opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, the first thing I look for is people who are genuinely obsessed with a problem, not just a technique. Biology has a ton of people who are excellent at one method, and that's valuable, but at Arc we're trying to work on things that take longer horizons and cut across disciplines. So I want someone who can tell me what they'd do if the method they love turned out to be the wrong tool. That tells you whether they're problem-driven or tool-driven.

The second thing is range. The most interesting work right now sits at the interface of experimental biology and computation: people training models on genomic or single-cell data, and people building the wet-lab systems that generate the data those models need. I don't expect everyone to be fluent in both, but I want people who are curious enough about the other side to have real conversations with their collaborators. The biologist should want to understand what the model is actually learning, and the ML person should care about what an experiment can and can't tell you.

Third, and this is maybe underrated, I look for taste. Can you pick a good problem? A lot of very smart people spend years on questions that are either intractable or don't matter much if they succeed. Good scientific taste means finding the things that are just becoming possible because of some new capability, whether that's a new perturbation technology, a better sequencing readout, or a model that suddenly works at scale, and moving quickly on them.

And finally, I care a lot about ambition paired with low ego. We give people a lot of freedom and resources, and the point is for them to take big swings. But big swings in science mostly fail, so you need people who can be wrong, say so quickly, share what they learned, and get back to work. The people who thrive tend to be the ones who are excited about the team succeeding, not just about whose name ends up on the paper.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, the first thing I look for is taste. Not credentials, not pedigree. Can this person look at a messy, open-ended problem and pick the version of it that actually matters? A lot of people are very good at executing once a question has been handed to them. Far fewer are good at deciding which question to ask in the first place, and at Arc that's really the whole job, because we've deliberately removed a lot of the external structure that normally does that deciding for you. There are no grant cycles telling you what to work on. So if you don't have a strong internal compass for what's important, that freedom is actually paralyzing.

The second thing is a kind of fearlessness about tools. The people who have worked best for us are the ones who don't see a hard boundary between wet lab and computation, or between biology and engineering. If the right experiment requires writing a few thousand lines of code, or building a piece of hardware, or learning a technique from a totally different field, they just go do it. They treat their skill set as something that expands to fit the problem rather than something the problem has to fit into. That's become even more important as machine learning has started to eat a lot of what we do. Someone who can go back and forth between a model's predictions and a plate of cells is worth a lot more than two specialists who have to translate for each other.

And then the third thing, which is harder to interview for, is whether they're genuinely drawn to the frontier or just to being near it. There's a difference between wanting to work on exciting problems and being willing to be wrong in public for two years while you figure one out. We ask people to describe projects that failed, and I pay a lot of attention to whether they understand why it failed and what they'd do differently, versus whether they've just repackaged it into a success story. The ones who can sit with the failure honestly are usually the ones who end up doing the really interesting work.

I'd also say we try pretty hard to look past the proxies. The best person we've hired in a given year is often someone whose CV wouldn't have made it through a traditional faculty search. They did something weird, or they switched fields, or they spent time in industry doing something that looked like a detour. Those detours are usually where the taste comes from.

astra-6.text:
I look for people who have strong scientific taste—people who can identify an important question and explain why it matters. Beyond technical ability, I want to understand how they think when there isn’t a clear path forward. Can they challenge their own assumptions? Can they learn something new when the problem demands it?

I also care a lot about collaboration. Science involves a tremendous amount of uncertainty, and you want colleagues who are ambitious about the work, generous with their ideas, and willing to change their minds. A useful conversation is to ask someone what they’re most excited about, what they’ve tried, and what surprised them. That can tell you much more than a list of accomplishments.

sol-6.1.text:
I look for people who have a strong sense of curiosity and independent taste in scientific problems. Can they identify an important question, explain why it matters, and think creatively about how to answer it? I’m interested in how someone thinks when the answer isn’t obvious, and what they do when an experiment challenges their assumptions.

And then there’s the collaborative aspect. Science is a team effort, so I look for people who are generous with their ideas, open to feedback, and excited to learn from colleagues with very different expertise. You want people who can push an idea forward while also being willing to change their minds.
